checkpoints.title: Tradeoff duel
checkpoints.prompt: You must run untrusted user code. Where?

options.label: A plain Docker container
options.verdict: Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel exploit is a host compromise — and you are inviting the entire internet to run arbitrary code. Fine for isolating your own workloads, not for hostile ones.

options.label: gVisor or a Firecracker microVM
options.verdict: A second boundary between the guest and the host kernel. You pay roughly 125ms of cold start, which is why you keep a warm pool rather than booting per submission.

defend.prompt: What does the sandbox still need around it?

options.label: Hard CPU, memory and wall-clock limits
No outbound network from the guest
A pre-warmed pool to hide cold starts
Trusting the submitted code to terminate

defend.explain: Assuming termination is exactly the mistake — infinite loops are the common case, not the exception. The runner kills on wall-clock regardless of what the code thinks it is doing.

checkpoints.title: Capacity ladder
checkpoints.prompt: Judging a submission inside a five-second end-to-end SLA.

rungs.q: Cold start for a hardened microVM
rungs.note: Which is a large slice of a five-second budget if paid per submission.
Pre-warmed runners bring effective start-up under 100ms.
Which is why execution is queued rather than synchronous.

checkpoints.explain: The SLA is achievable only because the expensive part — a booted, isolated runtime — is prepared before the submission arrives.

checkpoints.title: Architecture builder
checkpoints.explain: The submission is accepted and queued immediately so a contest spike never blocks the API. Workers pull at their own rate and execute inside the sandbox. Results and leaderboards are written afterwards — the client polls or is pushed, rather than holding a connection open for five seconds.

checkpoints.title: Spot the bottleneck
checkpoints.prompt: During a contest, submissions queue for minutes. CPU across the worker fleet sits at 30%.
checkpoints.explain: Workers are idle at 30% CPU while the queue grows, so they are blocked rather than saturated — they are waiting on a sandbox to run code in. The warm pool is exhausted, so every submission now pays a full cold boot serially. Scale the pool ahead of contest start; worker CPU was never the limit.

wrong.Worker Pool: 30% CPU is the symptom of waiting. Ask what they are waiting for.
wrong.Queue: Depth is the consequence of slow drain, not the cause.
wrong.API Gateway: Submissions are being accepted quickly — they just are not being executed.
